item.title: Dem senator swipes credit for bill he opposed amid heated reelection bid: 'Disturbing pattern'
item.description: Jon Ossoff touted Georgia military construction wins at Fort Benning and Fort Stewart despite voting against the bill that funded those improvements.
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., is touting his advocacy for federal investment in Georgia military infrastructure despite having ultimately voted against the bill that secured the improvements.

Most recently, Ossoff highlighted new construction for an elementary school at Fort Benning, improved conditions at Fort Stewart, pay raises for military personnel and improvements to Georgia’s foster care system — all a part of the annual military funding bill known as Military Construction and Veteran Affairs (MilCon-VA).

At the time of its initial passage, Ossoff quickly released a press statement.

FOX NEWS POLL: AN EARLY LOOK AT THE GEORGIA SENATE RACE

"U.S. Senate passes Sen. Ossoff’s Bipartisan Bill that provides most funding for Georgia military construction in 15 years," his website announced.

When reconsidering it for final passage, Ossoff opposed the package.

Notably, Ossoff, as the ranking member on the Senate Subcommittee on Military Construction and Veteran Affairs, voted in favor of the bill in committee and as a standalone bill, but opposed its final passage later that year when it was bundled together with other government funding legislation. 

When asked about the voting record, his office reaffirmed the federal support secured in Georgia.

"Let's be clear: Georgia's massive 2026 military construction budget, the highest in 15 years, is a direct and undeniable result of Senator Ossoff's work as the senior Democrat on the Military Construction subcommittee," an Ossoff campaign spokesperson told Fox News Digital in a statement.

"Senator Ossoff makes no apology for having tried to stop Mike Collins from doubling premiums for more than a million Georgians and throwing 300,000 off their health insurance," they added, referring to Ossoff's Republican challenger, Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., and caps on federal health subsidies Republicans had championed at the time of MilCon-VA's passage.

Like many Democrats, Ossoff has struggled to oppose legislation championed by President Donald Trump while at the same time making his case for reelection in one of the country’s most competitive Senate seats. Ossoff won in 2021 with a 50.6% to 49.4% victory over Republican incumbent Sen. David Perdue, R-Ga.

In the case of the elementary school, Ossoff said he had been calling for those investments for years.

"I have been working for years now for a replacement for Dexter Elementary. That’s really important for those families down there in Columbus," Ossoff said. "I’m just a bit concerned by the lack of attention in this year’s base budget, so we’ll work together on that."

Ossoff made similar remarks about improvements to Fort Stewart, citing concerns in press releases about lead exposure affecting newborns' health on the base, mold contamination and flooded living areas.

Ossoff released findings in a seven-page report about the base’s conditions.

SEN. BLUMENTHAL, REP. TAKANO: CONGRESS CAN FUND VETERANS’ CARE WITHOUT TAKING BENEFITS FROM DISABLED HEROES

"Our military service members and their families make huge sacrifices for the country, and it’s a travesty how they’re being treated by privatized housing contractors in Georgia and nationwide," Sen. Ossoff said.

"The stories in this report should shock our conscience, and I will continue exposing the mistreatment of military families in privatized housing and working to protect them and improve conditions."

Notably, the package Ossoff ultimately voted against contained $8 million for Fort Stewart and $127.4 million to replace the Dexter Elementary School.

A veteran lawmaker ripped Ossoff for highlighting wins he didn’t participate in.

"Last year, he tried to take credit for my veterans housing bill, legislation he had absolutely nothing to do with. A politician who tries to erase a veteran’s work for political gain has forfeited the trust of the people he seeks to represent," Rep. Derrick Van Orden, R-Wisc., said in a statement, referring to a bill he introduced last year.

Ossoff highlighted the bill on his website, calling it a "bipartisan bill backed by U.S. Senator Jon Ossoff" and announcing that "Sen. Ossoff brings Republicans and Democrats together to protect veterans from foreclosure."  

Ossoff was not a sponsor of the bill and, because it passed unanimously in a voice vote, did not cast a vote for it either.

DEM SENATOR ACCUSED OF BEING 'NOWHERE TO BE FOUND' ON CRUCIAL ISSUE IMPACTING KIDS IN SWING STATE

"Ossoff’s disturbing pattern of taking credit for work he didn’t do and claiming victories he didn’t support demonstrates both gross incompetence and a complete lack of integrity," Van Orden said.

item.title: 'Lord of the Rings' star Sean Astin had to sell his home after negotiating 'small' salary for hit movie
item.description: Sean Astin reveals he had to sell his house after negotiating a surprisingly small salary for the "Lord of the Rings" trilogy with no residuals.
item.content:encoded:
Sean Astin captured the hearts of fantasy fans everywhere when he starred as Samwise Gamgee in the "Lord of the Rings," but says the compensation was not what one would expect.

In a new interview with The Guardian, the 55-year-old actor shared just how "small" his payday was for the incredibly successful Academy Award-winning trilogy.

"I was not prepared for that level of visibility and access," he said. "And there was a disconnect between the attention that I was getting and how much money we had. It was not a lot of money! In fact, I had to sell my house because I negotiated such a small amount on the trilogy."

He previously revealed in a November 2017 interview on the "Jim and Sam Show" that he made $250,000 for his work on the trilogy, alongside some profit from merchandise sales, but no residuals.

'MARRIED... WITH CHILDREN' STAR TED MCGINLEY REVEALS HE GETS PENNY RESIDUAL CHECKS FROM HIS HIT TV SHOWS

The "Stranger Things" star went on to say that he had purchased a home in Los Angeles and was told he needed to make $250,000 a year to pay the mortgage when he got the role in the films.

"It was an offer for $250,000 for a year and a half," he said. "And I was like, ‘Wait a minute, my pen signed this contract, which obligated me to $250,000 a year, and I’m gonna sign this contract, which will make it so that I absolutely cannot satisfy that other thing.'"

He went on to say that in the end was all about negotiating. He also clarified that by the time the third movie was released, he "was feeling a little bit better" in terms of finances, adding that "By then, I had done a lot of other work, and we were fine."

Astin's co-star in the first installment of the trilogy, Cate Blanchett, who played Galadriel, also spoke about how little she was paid for her role, telling Andy Cohen in an August 2024 episode of "Watch What Happens Live," "No one got paid anything to do that movie."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"I wanted to work with the guy who made 'Braindead,'" she said about why she took the role despite the low pay. "I mean I basically got free sandwiches. And I got to keep my ears, which is something."

Other cast members, including Orlando Bloom and Elijah Wood, have also spoken about how little they were paid for their work in the films, with Bloom telling Howard Stern in 2019 that he was paid $175,000 for the trilogy.

Also starring Viggo Mortensen, Sean Bean and Ian McKellen, the trilogy went on to become a huge blockbuster success.

The first film, "Fellowship of the Ring," raked in about $897 million at the worldwide box office, with its sequels bringing in about $945 million and $1.15 billion respectfully.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

All three films were also critically acclaimed, earning a combined 30 Academy Award nominations and 17 wins. The third film alone, "Return of the King," won all 11 categories it was nominated in, including best picture, tying the record for the most Oscars won by a single film.

item.title: Billy Ray Smith, top 5 NFL draft pick, dead at 64; family says CTE caused dementia
item.description: Billy Ray Smith's family says the College Football Hall of Famer faced a long journey with dementia caused by CTE before his death at age 64.
item.content:encoded:
Former San Diego Chargers linebacker Billy Ray Smith died this week at the age of 64, his family announced.

The family said Smith, a College Football Hall of Famer, "faced [a] long journey with dementia caused by CTE."

Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) is a progressive, degenerative brain disease linked to repeated head impacts rather than a single injury, according to the Mayo Clinic. 

More than 100 former NFL players have been posthumously diagnosed with CTE, according to a University of Utah study published in the Journal of Neurotrauma.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

"Billy Ray brought so much joy, light, and laughter to the world as a devoted father, husband, son, and loyal friend," the family said in a statement, adding that he fought his illness "with unmatched bravery, dignity, and strength."

This year, the families of Aldon Smith, Steve McMichael and Claude Lemieux have all said the former athletes' brains will be sent for CTE research. Smith's cause of death is still pending, while Lemieux died by suicide by hanging and McMichael suffered from ALS. 

Former running back Chris Johnson revealed earlier this year he, too, had been diagnosed with ALS.

BEARS LEGEND BRIAN URLACHER TALKS TEAM'S LIKELY MOVE, USC SON'S COLLEGE CAREER

CTE can only be officially diagnosed after death.

"To know Billy Ray was to love Billy Ray. Yes, he was a member of our 50th Anniversary team. Yes, he was a Charger for life, playing his entire 10-year career here," Chargers owner Dean Spanos said in a statement. "But he wasn't merely a great football player. He was, truly, larger than life. Always smiling. Lighting up every room he walked into. Infectious laughter. The kind of friend a friend should be. That was Billy Ray.

"When someone who brought so much positivity into the world leaves us, it's hard to process. Hard to accept. That's how I feel right now, and I know I'm not alone.

"Billy Ray loved his family, loved the Chargers, loved his teammates, loved his community and loved helping those in need. And we all loved him back," Spanos added. "Our hearts are with his wife, Kimberly; daughter, Savannah; and the countless people whose lives were made just a little bit brighter because they had the privilege of knowing Billy Ray."

Smith played 10 seasons with the Chargers after being drafted with the No. 5 overall pick of the 1983 NFL draft out of Arkansas. He was named to the Chargers' 50th anniversary team after racking up 15 career interceptions, 14 fumble recoveries and 13 forced fumbles.

If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Tim Robbins turns to ayahuasca after feeling 'consumed by anger' over cancel culture
item.description: Tim Robbins tells Joe Rogan how an ayahuasca ceremony helped him release years of frustration over cancel culture and political polarization.
item.content:encoded:
Oscar-winning actor Tim Robbins says an ayahuasca trip helped him break free from the anger he felt over America's deep divide.

Robbins revealed the psychedelic experience left him feeling "completely lighter" after years of frustration with cancel culture and political polarization.

The "Shawshank Redemption" star said he turned to the Amazonian psychedelic brew with one goal in mind — to stop being "consumed" by outrage over what he sees as the unraveling of modern society.

KELSEY GRAMMER SUSPECTS HE 'MAY HAVE' LOST HOLLYWOOD ROLES DUE TO CONSERVATIVE VIEWS

"They tell you to go in with an intention," Robbins said during a candid appearance on "The Joe Rogan Experience." "My intention was to … I was frustrated with feeling anger about what was going on in the world, and I said, 'I want to release that. I don't want to be consumed by that anger.'"

Robbins said his psychedelic experience was an intense spiritual journey that included what he described as an encounter with his late mother.

"What she said was, 'You're injured. You're a warrior, and you're injured and you need to rest, but the fight's not over,'" Robbins recalled.

When Joe Rogan asked what battle he believed he was fighting, Robbins pointed squarely at today's culture wars.

"I was battling my frustration with the dissolution of society, people being angry at each other over ridiculous things, long friendships being affected, people being canceled for expressing their opinion, all this stuff," he said. "And I wanted out. I wanted to be absolved of that. I didn't want to be engaged in it."

Although Robbins acknowledged skeptics would dismiss the experience, he said it profoundly changed him.

"I definitely felt her presence there. It was no doubt it was her," he said, adding that by the end of the ceremony he felt "completely lighter" and reconnected with his late mother.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Earlier in the conversation, Robbins also spoke about the hot-button issue, arguing that cancel culture bears striking similarities to tactics used under the former Soviet Union.

The actor recalled touring Eastern Europe with his play "Topsy Turvy," where he asked audience members in Romania what aspects of modern life reminded them of the communist era.

"They said, 'Without a doubt, cancel culture,'" Robbins recounted.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

According to Robbins, audience members described how Soviet authorities allegedly kept damaging personal files on citizens and weaponized them against anyone who stepped out of line.

"'Well, Soviet Union used to keep files on all of us, right?'" he recalled the person saying. "'So, as long as you're a good party member, there wouldn't be a thing said. But once you stepped out of line, they brought out that old file. Now that affair with your secretary from 30 years ago is going to ruin your life. They're going to ruin your family. They're going to kill your career. And they're going to make a big public display of it to show other people to stay in line.'"

"They felt like cancel culture was basically operating in the same way as the Soviet Union did," Robbins said. "It was really interesting to see that perspective in Eastern Europe — people that have, you know, lived under that kind of oppressive situation and their perspective on modern day."

Robbins has been a fixture in Hollywood for more than four decades, winning the Academy Award for best supporting actor for 2003's "Mystic River" and starring in films including "The Shawshank Redemption," "Bull Durham" and "Top Gun."

He also founded the Los Angeles theater company The Actors' Gang and has become increasingly outspoken in recent years, criticizing COVID-19 lockdowns and vaccine mandates.

item.title: Trump pushes F-35 sale to Turkey, but his own State Department says Erdoğan hasn't met legal requirements
item.description: A State Department letter to Congress confirms Turkey has not met legal conditions for the F-35, despite Trump's promise to lift sanctions on Ankara.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump has opened the door to selling Turkey the U.S.' prized F-35 fighter jet, praising Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and promising to remove sanctions imposed over Ankara’s purchase of a Russian missile defense system.

But a State Department letter to Congress makes clear that Turkey has not taken the steps legally required to receive the advanced fighter.

"Turkey has not yet met these conditions," the department said in the July 22 letter, first obtained by the Greek newspaper Kathimerini.

TRUMP COULD HAND PRIZED STEALTH JETS TO NATO ALLY ONCE SEEN AS ALLIANCE HEADACHE

The letter said U.S. law prohibits the transfer of F-35 aircraft to Turkey until Ankara no longer possesses the Russian-made S-400 system or associated equipment, promises not to acquire it again and satisfies the remaining certification requirements established by Congress.

The finding came weeks after Trump stood alongside Erdoğan at the NATO summit in Ankara and said his administration would lift sanctions on Turkey and consider selling it the aircraft.

Asked about Turkey’s continued possession of the S-400, Trump said, "I have no concerns about anything having to do with Turkey."

Trump described relations with Ankara as "better probably than it’s ever been," said Turkey had been "much more loyal" than some other countries and called a potential F-35 sale "certainly something we will consider."

Erdoğan said Turkey previously has been promised five aircraft and expressed confidence in Trump.

"I know that Mr. Trump always keeps his promises," Erdoğan said, according to Reuters.

The dispute matters far beyond a single weapons sale.

Turkey is a pivotal NATO ally controlling access between Europe and the Middle East, but its ties to Russia and Hamas have fueled doubts in Washington about whether Ankara can be trusted with America’s most sensitive military technology. The outcome will test whether Trump’s personal relationship with Erdoğan can bring Turkey back into the Western defense fold — or whether Congress and national security concerns will block the deal.

WHO IS TURKEY'S RECEP TAYYIP ERDOĞAN? HOW NATO'S MOST UNPREDICTABLE LEADER KEEPS REINVENTING HIMSELF

A State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital on background that Trump "recognizes the strategic importance of Türkiye" and that his administration is encouraging Ankara "to resolve pending issues."

"Türkiye is a valued NATO ally, and we continue to engage on all aspects of our important and multi-faceted relationship," the spokesperson said.

James Jeffrey, a former U.S. ambassador to Turkey and former special representative for Syria engagement, said Trump’s position reflects both his trust in Erdoğan and their cooperation on regional security issues.

"Trump is very much for this as he works well with Erdoğan and trusts him and has succeeded together on a host of security issues from Libya to Syria to Caucasus to Ukraine and PKK ceasefire with Ankara," Jeffrey, now a distinguished fellow at The Washington Institute, told Fox News Digital.

"He knows how important this is to Erdoğan and all Turks and doesn’t want Ankara to turn to Russia or China for weapons," he said.

Turkey was removed from the F-35 development program in 2019 after purchasing the S-400 from Russia. The United States imposed sanctions the following year under the Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act.

U.S. officials have argued that operating the Russian system alongside the F-35 could allow Moscow to collect sensitive information about the stealth aircraft.

Jeffrey said Turkey would have to genuinely relinquish the S-400 but noted that the law does not specify exactly how.

"Certainly transferring to another country would meet the legal and technical requirement," he said.

Sinan Ciddi, director of the Turkey Program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, agreed that a third-country transfer could begin the process of restoring Turkey to the program. But he said Ankara would also have to provide guarantees that it would not again seek major Russian military equipment or maintain ties that could compromise the aircraft.

TRUMP BETS ON FORMER NATO TROUBLEMAKER AS TURKEY'S STRATEGIC VALUE SURGES

Reports have suggested the United Arab Emirates as a possible destination for the S-400. Ciddi said, however, that there is no confirmation Abu Dhabi would accept it.

The UAE would have to consider whether acquiring the Russian system could trigger U.S. penalties or jeopardize access to other American weapons, he said. Russia could also object to Turkey transferring the system without Moscow’s approval.

Jeffrey said Erdoğan is likely prepared to resist Russian pressure because the F-35 is both a prestige issue and an important military need for Turkey, whose air force relies heavily on F-16 aircraft.

Ciddi argued that resolving the S-400 dispute should not automatically clear the way for a sale.

"The S-400 issue that led to Turkey’s removal from the F-35 program is the floor, not the ceiling," Ciddi said, pointing to Ankara’s relationship with Hamas, continued ties with Russia, use of Chinese telecommunications technology and tensions with U.S. partners including Greece, Cyprus and Israel as additional obstacles.

The State Department letter reflected the administration’s competing views of Ankara.

While reiterating that Turkey remains legally ineligible for the F-35, the department credited it with supporting US diplomatic efforts involving Russia and Ukraine, Azerbaijan and Armenia, Gaza and counter-ISIS operations.

The letter said Turkey used its relationship with Hamas’ political leadership to help secure acceptance of Trump’s Gaza peace plan and advance the first phase of a ceasefire.

At the same time, it warned that Hamas continues to use financial channels operating from Turkish territory.

"Hamas’ use of informal financial networks and unlicensed exchange houses in Turkey to access funds remains a concern, and we are committed to disrupting these illicit financing streams," the State Department said.

Jeffrey said those Hamas ties could generate opposition in Congress but may carry less weight with Trump because his administration has relied on Ankara in Gaza diplomacy.

Ciddi interpreted the letter not as a rejection of Turkey’s return, but as a signal that the administration is prepared to move forward if Ankara meets the legal requirements.

"I think the letter is trying to convey to Congress, ‘Look, once Turkey makes good on the legal requirements of the NDAA, we can proceed with the sale,’" he said.

Congress could still be the most significant obstacle. Lawmakers have prohibited the transfer while Turkey possesses the S-400, and a bipartisan group of 18 House members recently urged congressional leaders to block any sale under current conditions, according to Axios.

The issue also has regional implications. Israel reportedly has pressed Trump not to provide Turkey with the aircraft, amid fears that a sale could weaken Israel’s qualitative military edge as tensions between Erdoğan and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu deepen.

For now, the State Department’s message is clear: Trump may favor the sale, but Erdoğan must first surrender the Russian system that caused Turkey’s expulsion from the program.

The State Department and Turkish Embassy in Washington did not respond to Fox News Digital’s requests for comment.

item.title: Left-wing sports host Sarah Spain launches disgusting personal smear of Sophie Cunningham
item.description: Sarah Spain attacked Sophie Cunningham's character on her "Good Game" podcast and dismissed her documented felony stalking case as complaining.
item.content:encoded:
Sarah Spain wants everyone to know that she champions women.

She often refers to the NBA as the "MNBA," an incredibly performative way to make sure listeners understand that the WNBA isn’t some secondary league just because it has a "W" in front of it.

But listen to Spain talk about actual women, particularly women who disagree with her politically, and that supposed respect disappears rather quickly.

WNBA MEDIA PREDICTABLY EMBARRASSES ITSELF AGAIN BY IGNORING SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM STORY OVER ALL-STAR WEEKEND

Spain used a recent episode of her "Good Game" podcast to launch one of the most disgusting personal attacks I’ve heard against Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham. She didn’t simply disagree with Cunningham’s position on males competing in women’s sports. Spain attacked Cunningham’s character, motives, upbringing, family, friends and ability to care about anyone other than herself.

The best part? Spain’s own evidence completely contradicted her conclusion.

Spain read directly from a recent ESPN profile in which Cunningham explained why she opposes allowing biological males to compete against girls and enter their locker rooms.

"I think that I am here to extend love, but I also think that with love is truth, being honest, and I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport, who shouldn’t have to go against biological men," Cunningham said.

Seems fairly clear, right?

Cunningham wasn’t talking about protecting her own WNBA roster spot. She wasn’t complaining about having to compete against a male herself. She was expressing concern for young girls who have far less power, influence and ability to speak publicly than she does.

Spain somehow reached the exact opposite conclusion.

"It just seems like she doesn’t have any interest in empathizing or caring about anyone but Sophie," Spain said.

Did she listen to the quote she had just read?

Spain didn’t deliver the segment in a measured or analytical tone. Her voice dripped with contempt as she portrayed Cunningham as selfish, uncaring and the product of a family that encouraged her to make everything about herself.

"Cunningham has been emboldened throughout her life by family and supporters to be the center of her own story," Spain said.

This wasn’t simply a disagreement over transgender athletes. Spain was attacking Cunningham’s character and attempting to explain how the people closest to her had supposedly helped shape it.

Then Spain described Cunningham’s comments about protecting girls as "filled with offensive language" and "entirely lacking nuance or care."

Spain called Cunningham’s statement "filled with offensive language."

But what exactly was offensive?

Cunningham said she wanted to "extend love," speak the "truth," be "honest" and "protect young girls."

Yet, Spain used that statement as proof Cunningham lacks empathy.

Come on.

Cunningham’s quote was explicitly about other people. Spain’s accusation wasn’t merely unsupported. It was disproven by the quote Spain had just read.

Then Spain’s attack turned much darker.

Spain accused Cunningham of failing to discuss harassment directed toward other WNBA players and said, "She complains of stalkers, for instance."

"Complains."

Spain made it sound as though Cunningham were whining about nasty replies on social media or someone criticizing her basketball ability. That's an incredible minimization of what Cunningham actually faced.

An Indianapolis man was charged with felony stalking and intimidation, along with misdemeanor harassment, after prosecutors alleged that he targeted Cunningham over an extended period. The charges are allegations, and the man has not been convicted in the case.

According to court filings reviewed by OutKick and Fox News Digital, the man allegedly hand-delivered a package for Cunningham to Gainbridge Fieldhouse. Investigators said an account tied to him posted sexually explicit messages and references to his physical proximity to Cunningham, including a message stating, "You’re literally down the street from me!"

INDIANAPOLIS MAN CHARGED WITH ALLEGED STALKING OF INDIANA FEVER'S SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM, THREATENING SECURITY EXEC.

Cunningham told investigators that the continued posts caused her to stay home more often and suffer nightmares. She said she felt as though she constantly had to watch her back, didn’t feel safe and feared the man. Prosecutors said the conduct continued after Pacers Sports & Entertainment sent him a cease-and-desist letter and banned him from team properties and events.

The situation was so serious that the man was also accused of threatening John Ball, the Pacers security executive who intervened. One alleged message stated, "Pain is coming. I promise." Ball told investigators that the man referenced his wife and the county where he lived, causing him to alter his routine, begin carrying a firearm and request additional police patrols near his home.

That’s what Spain reduced to Cunningham "complaining."

And Spain didn’t mention the stalking because she felt sympathy for Cunningham. She used Cunningham’s terrifying experience as another piece of evidence against her. Apparently, Cunningham failed Spain’s test because she didn’t use her own documented stalking ordeal to center harassment directed at other WNBA players, particularly Black and queer players.

White players are expected to answer for every threat, insult or injustice involving Black players. But when Caitlin Clark or Sophie Cunningham is targeted, the conversation quickly becomes what those women have supposedly failed to do for someone else.

Spain didn’t forget that Cunningham had been stalked. She mentioned it herself.

She simply decided Cunningham wasn’t the kind of woman whose fear deserved empathy.

Later in the same episode, Spain made women’s fear and safety the foundation of an entirely different argument.

Spain and ESPN reporter Holly Rowe discussed whether WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert should personally provide more emotional support to players who receive harassment or threatening messages.

Rowe offered a fair solution: The league could employ a former player or dedicated player-relations official who knows the athletes, communicates with them directly and provides support when needed.

"I don’t necessarily know that it needs to come from the commissioner’s office," Rowe said. "I feel like Cathy should be worried about business, right?"

Spain initially claimed to agree. Then she argued that the WNBA commissioner may need to have a fundamentally different job than commissioners in other major professional leagues.

"I think in men’s sports, you would not expect the commissioner to have that necessarily direct line to the players," Spain said. "I do think maybe there’s an argument that this league needs it."

Spain suggested that Engelbert could become the CEO or president, while a former player could become "more the commissioner type" and handle the emotional relationships with players.

So, Spain’s position appears to be that male professional athletes can have a commissioner whose job is to run the business, represent ownership and absorb criticism. Female professionals, however, may require the title of commissioner to belong to someone whose primary role is tending more directly to the players’ emotions.

That's incredibly condescending.

A women’s league can and should have security officials, mental-health resources and player-relations employees. But the commissioner of a women’s professional sports league shouldn’t have a fundamentally different job simply because she's a woman or because the athletes are women.

Apparently, Spain believes adding an "M" to the NBA is equality. Treating female athletes like equally capable professionals is another matter.

And, for the record, calling it the "MNBA" isn’t merely silly. It’s factually incorrect because the NBA isn’t a male-only league.

Ann Meyers signed with the Indiana Pacers in 1979 and became the first woman to receive an NBA tryout. The league’s current collective bargaining agreement defines a player contract as an agreement between a "person" and a team.

A woman good enough to earn a roster spot with the New York Knicks would be eligible to play for the New York Knicks. The NBA is already the NBA. It doesn’t need Spain’s performative rebranding.

Spain apparently knew listeners might hear Rowe’s argument and conclude that Rowe was right.

Before playing the interview, Spain inserted a scripted clarification. She said she wanted to explain a point that she wasn’t sure "gets out fully in our convo."

Spain bundled trolling, racial and homophobic slurs, harassment and threats into one broad category. She argued that those issues make up an "outsized portion" of the conversation surrounding the WNBA, unlike in men’s sports.

"And that’s why I think the commissioner and the league have a different responsibility when it comes to addressing and communicating with the players about it," Spain said.

This wasn’t an off-the-cuff comment that came out poorly during a live discussion. Spain heard the interview, had time to reconsider her position, wrote a clarification and recorded it for listeners.

Given all that time, she doubled down.

That makes the Cunningham hypocrisy even more appalling. Less than half an hour after dismissing a real and extensively documented stalking case as something Cunningham "complains" about, Spain argued that women experience threats so differently that leaders of women’s sports require a different job description.

You couldn’t create a clearer double standard if you tried.

When the woman was Sophie Cunningham, Spain treated a stalking case involving criminal charges, sexually explicit messages, physical proximity and threats against security personnel as an annoyance.

When Spain discussed alleged online harassment involving players who better fit her racial and ideological narrative, female vulnerability suddenly became so important that the WNBA needed an entirely different kind of commissioner.

The facts didn’t determine Spain’s level of empathy.

The identity and politics of the woman did.

What makes the exchange with Rowe so compelling is that Rowe isn’t some conservative critic of Spain or the WNBA.

Quite the opposite.

During the same conversation, Rowe argued that society constantly tries to tear women down. She blamed much of the WNBA’s online toxicity on misogyny, called the league celebratory and inclusive and proudly noted that "the WNBA helped flip the Senate in this country."

She also accused critics of not wanting WNBA players to be "strong and powerful and connected and unified."

WNBA SUDDENLY WANTS TO STICK TO BASKETBALL AFTER YEARS OF MAKING POLITICS PART OF THE PRODUCT

So, this wasn’t an argument between two people with opposing worldviews. Rowe accepts nearly all of Spain’s progressive premises about women, misogyny and the WNBA.

She still thought Spain’s conclusion was sexist.

Rowe asked whether Roger Goodell is paid to absorb criticism directed at the NFL.

Spain responded, "One thousand percent."

"That is his job," Rowe replied. "So, what’s wrong with that?"

Spain then questioned whether the WNBA commissioner’s job is different because of "the intersectionality of women’s sports," the relationship between female players and leadership and the negative coverage surrounding the league.

Rowe pushed back that athletes in the NBA and NFL receive similar abuse, some of which is likely related to gambling rather than racism, homophobia or misogyny. Spain continued insisting that the WNBA was different.

"That’s why I think right now, at this moment in time, leadership in the WNBA has more of a responsibility for that than on the men’s side," Spain said.

Rowe forcefully rejected the argument.

"That’s so sexist," Rowe said. "Like, why? Why can’t we be just like the men? I just find that so problematic."

Rowe wasn’t joking. She wasn’t teasing Spain or engaging in friendly banter. She adamantly rejected the premise that a female commissioner should have a different job because she’s a woman overseeing female athletes.

And she was right.

Caught flat-footed by Rowe’s response, Spain pivoted from the commissioner’s job to women’s safety more broadly.

Spain said threats affect men and women differently because male athletes have more money and security.

"Flat out, it is more dangerous for women, and they feel more endangered when they get threats than men do, especially men in multimillion-dollar mansions with tons of security," Spain said.

Rowe came prepared with an obvious counterexample. She cited Philadelphia Eagles star Saquon Barkley, whose home had just been invaded while he and his family were inside. Police said the break-in occurred early Saturday while Barkley’s home was occupied; Barkley and his family were not physically harmed.

Apparently, the multimillion-dollar mansion didn’t create an invisible force field.

More importantly, Spain had changed the subject. They weren’t debating whether men and women always experience danger identically. They were discussing whether those differences require a female commissioner to perform a different, more nurturing job.

Rowe recognized the pivot immediately.

"That’s a whole different conversation," Rowe said. "That’s not actually what we were even talking about."

Rowe then worried that people would clip the exchange and misrepresent her argument. So, let’s be perfectly clear.

Rowe wasn’t saying women never experience misogyny, harassment or distinct safety concerns. She was saying those concerns don’t change the fundamental job of a professional sports commissioner.

That context doesn’t weaken Rowe’s criticism.

It makes it stronger.

Spain’s entire argument hinges on men and women being fundamentally different.

She argues that women experience danger differently, feel more endangered by threats and require a different relationship with league leadership. In her telling, the differences are significant enough to reconsider how an entire professional sports league should be structured.

But when Cunningham says biological differences matter in athletic competition and intimate locker rooms, Spain calls the statement offensive and devoid of care.

So, sex matters enough to justify a different job description for the commissioner of a women’s league, but not enough to preserve women’s sports and locker rooms for women.

You can’t have this both ways.

Spain treats sex as critically important when it allows her to portray women as vulnerable. Then she treats it as subordinate to gender identity when girls ask for fair competition and privacy.

That isn’t a coherent principle. It’s an ideological convenience.

And it leads directly back to Sophie Cunningham.

Spain read Cunningham expressing concern for young girls and called her selfish. She mentioned Cunningham’s documented stalking ordeal and used it against her. Then she spent the rest of the episode explaining how deeply women are affected by threats and why they require greater protection.

Spain claims to champion women, but her empathy seems entirely dependent on whether the woman agrees with Sarah Spain.

That isn’t feminism.

It’s hypocrisy, and it’s disgusting.

item.title: Andy Cohen blasts GOP senators over Fauci grilling, claims they were 'berating' him over 'imaginary crimes'
item.description: Andy Cohen accused Senate Republicans of a "war on science" after Anthony Fauci's heated hearing where he invoked the Fifth Amendment over 100 times.
item.content:encoded:
Bravo host Andy Cohen accused Senate Republicans of waging a "war on science" Wednesday on "Watch What Happens Live!" after lawmakers grilled Dr. Anthony Fauci for more than three hours during a Washington hearing about the federal government's response to the COVID-19 pandemic.

Cohen dismissed GOP senators' questions as an effort to hold Fauci responsible for offenses that did not exist.

"It goes to Dr. Anthony Fauci, who spent over three hours today being grilled, berated and sworn at by Senate Republicans over the imaginary crimes they want you to believe he committed during his management of the COVID-19 pandemic," Cohen said.

He awarded Fauci his "Mazel of the Day," praised his decades of public service and suggested lawmakers were envious of doctors and scientists.

TOP 5 MOMENTS FROM FAUCI'S HEARING: PAUL BOOTS LAWYER, MORENO ERUPTS AS CONTEMPT VOTE LOOMS

"Maybe our politicians are just jealous because doctors and scientists do the one thing they can’t ever seem to do: fix something," Cohen said.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, drew Cohen’s criticism after demanding that Fauci apologize to parents, business owners and others affected by pandemic-era restrictions. Moreno also condemned Fauci’s repeated refusal to answer senators’ questions.

"Who the f--- do you think you are?" Moreno asked Fauci during the hearing. "It is a total disgrace what you did to this country."

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Moreno communications director Reagan McCarthy defended the senator’s questioning and responded directly to Cohen.

FAUCI PRIVATELY TOOK CREDIT FOR COVID-19 LOCKDOWNS DESPITE PUBLIC DENIAL, NEWLY EXPOSED DIARY ENTRIES REVEAL

"Was it appropriate for Fauci to keep kids out of school and cost thousands of small business owners their livelihoods with nonsensical restrictions?" McCarthy said.

"Senator Moreno spoke for all Americans who were chastised for standing up to pandemic tyranny, and a government bureaucrat who unilaterally shut down the country should be able to handle a curse word."

Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment more than 100 times during the Senate hearing, declining to answer questions about COVID-19's origins, federally funded research, lockdown policies, vaccine guidance and entries from his pandemic-era diary.

Committee Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., disputed Fauci’s ability to invoke the Fifth Amendment after former President Joe Biden issued him a preemptive pardon and said the committee would vote on whether to hold him in contempt.

ANTHONY FAUCI'S PRIVATE DIARY AND EMAILS SHOW HE KNEW LOCKDOWNS FAILED AND PUSHED MASKS WITHOUT EVIDENCE

Fox News Digital reached out to Paul for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

The committee's ranking Democrat, Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., criticized Paul's handling of the proceeding and accused Republicans of seeking predetermined conclusions.

Cohen also praised Fauci's work combating HIV/AIDS and credited him with helping develop the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief. The State Department has credited PEPFAR with saving 26 million lives, and Harvard Medical School has described Fauci as one of the program's principal architects.

Cohen’s monologue generated some criticism on social media, with one user accusing him of being "in bed with big pharma" over his promotion of COVID vaccines.

item.title: Zoe Saldaña says Taylor Sheridan 'really sees women' as Lioness season three hits Paramount+
item.description: Zoe Saldaña praised Taylor Sheridan's ability to write complex women ahead of "Lioness" season three, pushing back on critics of his female characters.
item.content:encoded:
Zoe Saldaña is a big fan of the way Taylor Sheridan writes female characters.

Season three of "Lioness" starts this Sunday on Paramount+, and that means Saldaña is running it back as CIA operator Joe.

While "Lioness" might not pull the same attention as "Yellowstone," I think there's a strong argument to be made that it's Sheridan's best work.

LAYSLA DE OLIVEIRA TEASES ‘LIONESS’ SEASON 3 DEBUT WITH BEHIND-THE-SCENES PHOTOS

The show shines a light on the world of black operations in the CIA and military, with a focus on the women who serve in those shadowy and secretive roles.

One of the main (and completely unjustified) criticisms of Sheridan is that he can't write solid female characters. It's comical considering "Lioness" is about strong female characters, and Beth in "Yellowstone" might be the overall strongest character he's written on TV.

Now, Saldaña is making it crystal clear that Sheridan knows exactly what he's doing, and does it at a very high level.

ALI LARTER DEFENDS TAYLOR SHERIDAN'S WRITING OF FEMALE CHARACTERS, CALLING CRITICISM A 'FALSE NARRATIVE'

"If there’s one thing that I love the most, it’s men that really see women, and know how to write women. And, I’ve been very fortunate to work with a lot of creative men that do that," the "Lioness" star explained during an appearance on CBS Mornings on Wednesday.

She further added, "Taylor Sheridan writes great, complex, wholesome women that they may not be perfect, but then again, human beings weren’t made to be perfect. I love the fact that there is an accurate depiction of Joe. A woman that, in front of her team, she never breaks and she’s able to carry so much responsibility on her shoulders. And yet, when she’s in her private quarters, you see this human being grapple with just having to make everything work."

You can watch her full comments in the video below, and let me know your thoughts at David.Hookstead@outkick.com.

TAYLOR SHERIDAN'S NEW WAR MOVIE GETS MAJOR UPDATE, LEGENDARY DIRECTOR ATTACHED

Well said, Zoe. Well said. People who claim Sheridan can't write female characters have literally no idea what they're talking about.

It all stems back to Emily Blunt's FBI character in "Sicario," who is depicted as not really understanding the scope of the operation she's involved in.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS

Spoiler: That's the entire point of the movie!

She's not there because she's an expert. She's there because the CIA hitters and Delta Force team needed an FBI agent for legal cover, and they didn't want one asking questions.

You can check out the start of "Lioness" season three on Paramount+ this Sunday. Let me know your predictions at David.Hookstead@outkick.com.

item.title: Sen Darline Graham drops campaign video on heels of brother's funeral services amid tight primary timeline
item.description: Sen. Darline Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, dropped a campaign video in her run for U.S. Senate with President Donald Trump's endorsement.
item.content:encoded:
U.S. Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died earlier this month, posted a campaign video Thursday in which she described herself as a "conservative Republican" and declared that she is "ready to serve."

"Thank you all for your prayers. They provided strength through an incredibly difficult time. I'm honored to serve South Carolina and grateful for President Trump's endorsement. And I'll work hard every day to earn it," she said in the video.

"I'm a conservative Republican, and I believe this: Every life is precious. Men don't belong in women's sports. And only American citizens should vote in our elections. I'm Darline Graham. I approve this message, and I am ready to serve," she added.

DARLINE GRAHAM REVEALS WHAT TRUMP TOLD HER INSIDE OVAL OFFICE AFTER BROTHER LINDSEY'S DEATH

The video release Thursday came on the heels of funeral services to honor the late Sen. Lindsey Graham in Washington, D.C., Tuesday and in South Carolina on Wednesday. A press release explained that, after the service on Wednesday, July 29, there would be "a private family burial in Pickens County, South Carolina."

The new senator, who is running to win a full six-year Senate term, is facing a tight election schedule. The Aug. 11 South Carolina GOP U.S. Senate primary is less than two weeks away, and early voting begins Wednesday, 
Aug. 5.

Her social media posts featuring the campaign video said, "I'm ready to serve and I humbly ask for your support on August 11th."

At the end of the video, a notice appeared at the bottom of the frame that says, "PAID FOR BY NRSC AND AUTHORIZED BY DARLINE FOR SENATE."

Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died July 11, had won the June 9 Republican U.S. Senate primary in the Palmetto State while running for a fifth term.

South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster, a Republican, announced July 13 the appointment of Graham's sister to fill the remainder of her brother's Senate term. She was sworn in the next day.

DARLINE GRAHAM FOCUSES ON KITCHEN TABLE ISSUES AS SHE ANNOUNCES FULL-TERM SENATE BID

President Donald Trump issued a Truth Social post July 17 in which he declared he had asked the new senator to run in the upcoming August special Republican U.S. Senate primary contest.

"Darline, who comes from an absolutely incredible family, has been a WINNER all of her life and, should she accept, has my Complete and Total Endorsement in the Special Election for U.S. Senate in South Carolina — SHE WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN. RUN, DARLINE, RUN!" he declared in part of the post.

Graham told Fox News Channel's Sean Hannity during an interview July 20 that she would run. 

"I'm in," she said.

SEN DARLINE GRAHAM REVEALS WHETHER SHE WILL RUN FOR A FULL-TERM DURING 'HANNITY' EXCLUSIVE

"It’s official. I'm running to represent South Carolina in the United States Senate," she said in a July 20 post on X. "Today, I’m stepping forward to carry my brother Lindsey’s legacy on behalf of the people of South Carolina. President Trump told me, 'Run, Darline, Run.' 

"With his support, I'm running all the way through the finish line in November. I hope you'll join me," she noted, adding a link to her campaign site.

Darline Graham faces a crowded GOP primary with candidates including U.S. Reps. Ralph Norman and Russell Fry, former Gov. Mark Sanford and businessman Mark Lynch. Lynch challenged Lindsey Graham in the June primary and lost to the late senator.

item.title: 'Worst of the Worst' judges are sabotaging Trump's immigration agenda, top DHS official says
item.description: DHS General Counsel James Percival names federal judges he says are engaging in judicial activism to block Trump's immigration and deportation agenda.
item.content:encoded:
DHS General Counsel James Percival says Americans deserve to know which federal judges are repeatedly blocking the Trump administration's immigration agenda, accusing a small group of district judges of acting in "open defiance" of the Supreme Court and engaging in "naked political activism."

Percival has begun posting on X identifying federal district judges while accusing them of obstructing key portions of President Donald Trump's immigration agenda. Critics have argued the campaign improperly targets members of the judiciary.

"The American people hear about these terrible acts of judicial activism. I think what they don't often understand is this is not some epidemic that sort of crosses the entire judiciary," Percival said. "There are particular judges who are a problem in case after case after case."

Percival told Fox News Digital the effort is intended to educate the public — not intimidate judges — and highlights what he described as a handful of repeat offenders acting in "open defiance" of the Supreme Court or reaching outside their Article III authority.

DHS EVISCERATES MEDIA FOR ‘ABSOLUTE ABSURDITY’ OVER CONCERN ABOUT ‘WORST OF THE WORST’ ACTIVIST JUDGES LIST

Percival stressed that he does not believe the federal judiciary faces a systemic problem of defiance against the Supreme Court or the separation of powers, but said activist plaintiffs are adept at "forum shopping."

"They file in these locations, often with very sort of dubious arguments to [have their case heard] in that venue. And they do it to get the same judges over and over and again."

GOP SENATOR UNVEILS BOASBERG ACT TO STOP 'ROGUE' JUDGES FROM HANDPICKING TRUMP CASES

He pointed to one such case in which Biden-appointed Judge Brian Murphy in Boston stopped a deportation flight until the Supreme Court intervened.

Murphy issued a 2025 order limiting the federal government's ability to deport illegal immigrants to receptive "third countries."

A flight bound for South Sudan was grounded in Djibouti, where the criminal illegal immigrants were taken to a U.S. military base.

"I think we had eight aliens on this flight to South Sudan. One of them had raped a child. One of them had raped a mentally-disabled person. These were very bad people that should not be in our country. And this Judge Brian Murphy was stopping us from doing this."

SUPREME COURT WEIGHS TRUMP EFFORT TO TERMINATE TEMPORARY PROTECTIONS FOR HAITIAN, SYRIAN MIGRANTS

DHS petitioned the Supreme Court to intervene. Percival said the incident drew support from liberal Justice Elena Kagan, who sided with the Trump administration in the case.

"She said, ‘Even though I disagreed the first time, I do agree that Judge Murphy can't defy the U.S. Supreme Court’," Percival said. "And so when you see the same judge doing these acts of sabotage on TPS (Temporary Protected Status), we just think it's important for the American people to understand."

"And this is not an attempt by me to blast the entire judiciary. It's just the opposite. If I were a member of the judiciary, I would want people to know this is a handful of district judges who are causing the same problems over and over and over again and calling the credibility of the entire branch of government into question when many of these judges are following the law and doing their jobs."

Percival now frequently shares the "Worst of the Worst" judges series, separate from ICE's "Worst of the Worst" criminal illegal immigrants series.

"If you think about DHS' "Worst of the Worst" series, the main purpose of that is just to inform the American public about what's going on," he said.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"There's a lot of false narratives out there about immigration enforcement, but when we actually show people the types of people we're moving from our communities, we think that really makes a big difference to the public..."

Percival said both series are intended to educate the public about DHS operations and counter narratives that do not reflect the agency's day-to-day work.

Percival highlighted Clinton-appointed Illinois Judge Matthew Kennelly — who issued an order pausing termination of TPS for Burma nationals.

"He did so even though these decisions are not subject to judicial review, even though we have been vindicated by the Supreme Court on TPS four times, and even though the Seventh Circuit summarily reversed him on the same issue only days before," Percival said in a separate statement.

"This is judicial sabotage."

He also called out Obama-appointed Judge Paula Xinis in Greenbelt, Maryland.

Percival called Xinis the reason Kilmar Abrego Garcia — the illegal immigrant the press dubbed "Maryland Man" and whom Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., had boat drinks with in El Salvador — is still in the U.S.

"She entered an order preventing his removal and then ordered him released on the basis that we had no plans to remove him. If it sounds crazy, it’s because it is. Our efforts to reverse this decision remain pending," Percival tweeted.

He said Biden-appointed Judge Hernan Vera in Los Angeles has "micromanage[d]" DHS' use-of-force policy by describing violent anti-ICE agitators as "legal observers" while deeming the agency "violent."

"[T]here's a lot of times when the American public thinks that there's something DHS is not doing because we're choosing not to do it," he said in his Fox News Digital interview.

"We just think it's very helpful for people to understand what we're facing in the courts, how out of control they are."

He noted there has been public frustration at the appearance of DHS not doing certain things or not going in as hard on others as promised, pointing to the wind-down of TPS for foreign nationals.

"Of course, a lot of that is because of the judicial sabotage that we are facing in district courts and in other [places]."

Fox News Digital reached out to the judges' respective courts for comment.

The media has also criticized Percival for the lists, including a Chicago Sun-Times reporter who asked whether the catalog he posted on X risks increasing threats against the judiciary.

"Witness the absolute absurdity of the liberal media response... Legitimate fact-based critiques of judges and their rulings is fair-game in a free society. Also, the media has no issue with it if the judge is conservative," Percival wrote.

He told Fox News Digital the issue is "classic separation-of-powers" in that the executive is allowed to tell another branch there’s disagreement.

Percival spoke with Fox News Digital from San Juan, where he was visiting personnel from Homeland Security Investigations.

He said HSI functions like an immigration-focused FBI, adding that it and other agencies reflect the "broad portfolio" he oversees as DHS's top lawyer.

"ICE is in the news the most, and so I think people are starting to associate me with ICE, but I love all my proverbial children equally. And I'm very dedicated to helping every single operator that my people are providing legal advice to be successful," he said, noting there are 50 DHS attorneys in Puerto Rico alone and that he felt it important to meet with them.

Critics' concerns about Percival's list come after other officials have also faced criticism for their rhetoric targeting certain judges.

Sen. Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., was criticized for claiming that Justices Brett Kavanaugh and Neil Gorsuch "released the whirlwind" by ruling against abortion protections in an incident that drew a rare public rebuke from Chief Justice John Roberts.

Kavanaugh, as well as Justice Amy Coney Barrett, have also been the target of threats from activist critics.

item.title: Jimmy Hoffa's family marks 51 years since iconic disappearance
item.description: The FBI says the Jimmy Hoffa disappearance case remains active 51 years later as his family pushes for accountability in the unsolved cold case.
item.content:encoded:
Jimmy Hoffa disappeared 51 years ago today, and his family has not given up hope that the answers to their painful loss will finally come.

"We want the case solved," Hoffa's son, James P. Hoffa, the former five-term president of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, told Fox News. "The family wants to have accountability for this horrible crime. We want the case solved so that the family can have closure."

Despite the passage of time, the FBI says the case remains ongoing and active. The bureau’s Detroit office is in charge of the case.

"The FBI has worked for five decades to investigate Jimmy Hoffa's disappearance, following every lead and carefully examining all evidence related to this investigation," the bureau said in a statement to Fox News.

TIPSTER CHARGED WITH MURDER AFTER POLICE SAY ANONYMOUS CALL HELPED SOLVE 30-YEAR DISAPPEARANCE

"If the public has any new, credible information regarding the disappearance of Jimmy Hoffa, the FBI will investigate," the FBI said.

Hoffa vanished on this day in 1975 as he was on his way to what he thought was a meeting to help his bid to regain the Teamsters union presidency. He was last seen in the parking lot of the Bloomfield Hills, Michigan, restaurant, the Machus Red Fox, at about 2:30 p.m. getting into a car that whisked him away. It is believed that the Detroit Mafia kidnapped and killed him to stop his efforts to take back the union.

SAMMY 'THE BULL' REVEALS WHY HIS LOVE FOR JOHN GOTTI TURNED INTO PRISON HATE

The eight-part documentary series, "Riddle, The Search for James R. Hoffa," streaming on Fox Nation, focuses on a dominant theory. It says that Hoffa was picked up at the restaurant by Detroit mob capo Vito "Billy Jack" Giacalone, who, along with mobster Anthony "Tony Pal" Palazzolo, drove Hoffa to a nearby home owned by mobster Carlo Licata and murdered him. His remains were then possibly disposed of in a mob-run sanitation facility in Hamtramck.

Hoffa believes that his father was picked up at the restaurant by Giacalone, but beyond that, he will not speculate about who killed his father.

Fox Nation's "Riddle" series reported that an informant told the FBI that he was present when Hoffa was murdered and said that Giacalone killed him. Such information would have been documented in the FBI records, called 302s, but so far the information has not been made public.

Detroit journalist and mob historian Scott Burnstein, who runs the website "Gangster Report," has confirmed that the 302 exists and reported that "confidential informants" told the FBI "that ‘Tony Pal’ was the ‘doer’" in the Hoffa homicide conspiracy, and that Giacalone "headed the Hoffa hit team and was present at the time Palazzolo kidnapped and clipped Hoffa."

COVERT DNA SAMPLE FROM COLORADO MAN'S TRASH REVIVES 44-YEAR-OLD TEXAS MURDER CASE: REPORT

Hoffa said that he has been aware of the information that Giacalone murdered his father but cannot confirm that. He does say that his dad was lured to the meeting by Giacalone and his brother Anthony "Tony Jack" Giacalone, who was considered the Detroit mob's street boss. Both men have since died.

In a letter to FBI Director Kash Patel obtained by Fox News, Hoffa wrote last month, "It is important to us and the country that the truth about my father's disappearance (be) told and those involved in his disappearance, even if they are deceased, be exposed."

Through the years there have been a variety of claims about Hoffa's fate.

Fox Nation's series investigated the claims of Frank Sheeran, "The Irishman," which proved to be unfounded. It's also been said that Hoffa's remains were buried in a mob-owned garbage dump in the New Jersey Meadowlands, but the FBI dug at the site in 2022 and came up empty. Stories have circulated that he was cremated or entombed in the downtown Detroit Renaissance Center office building complex.

New claims continue to crop up.

Independent investigator Roscoe Clark told Fox News that he is certain that Hoffa is buried in an undisclosed location in Michigan, and that it would take less than five minutes.

"Forensics will help solve the Jimmy Hoffa cold case," Clark said. "A team of experts is ready to move forward because of a lack of action by law enforcement. A location has been identified within three feet," and he said the necessary locating equipment is ready to be deployed.

The FBI said it has "received countless tips and information from the public, which have been a tremendous help to the FBI. We are grateful to the public, and most importantly, for the Hoffa's family assistance and support over the years."

UNIVERSITY OF PITTSBURGH STUDENTS SAY SUDIKSHA KONANKI'S 'CRAZY' DISAPPEARANCE COULD 'HAPPEN TO ANYBODY'

Observers note that the legacy of Jimmy Hoffa is not what happened to him, but what he accomplished. His hard-fought victories at the bargaining table and on the picket lines enabled generations to enjoy the American Dream, with healthcare and benefits, good pay and retirement. Millions of sons and daughters and their families still benefit from the feisty labor leader's achievements. In some ways, that is how Jimmy Hoffa is still with us, even as he is still deeply missed and mourned by his family.

James Hoffa, his sister Barbara, their adult children and grandchildren somberly mark this day with each passing year.

Every July 30 "is a hard day," said James Hoffa. "We always spend time with it. It is special time, a time to remember. The good thing is, that I had a great father and he did a great job in raising our family. He was a great man and we miss him."

The in-depth series "Riddle, The Search for James R. Hoffa," is streaming on Fox Nation.

item.title: WNBA admits controversial betting video featuring Angel Reese, Paige Bueckers 'missed the mark'
item.description: A deleted video shows Paige Bueckers and Angel Reese making a $400 wager on their own game, yet the WNBA dismisses it as simply lighthearted.
item.content:encoded:
The WNBA doesn't appear to be taking what could be a direct violation of its own anti-gambling policy very seriously whatsoever.

Ahead of Wednesday night's matchup between the Dallas Wings and Atlanta Dream, the WNBA's official X account shared a video showing Dallas' Paige Bueckers and Atlanta's Angel Reese – two of the league's most well-known players – making a $400 wager on the game. The WNBA was quick to delete the post, but not before many were able to share and also capture recordings of the video.

A WNBA spokesperson released a statement on Thursday claiming that the quickly deleted video was "intended to be lighthearted," but that it "simply missed the mark."

WNBA COMMISSIONER VOWS TO CRACK DOWN ON 'RACISM, MISOGYNY,' DODGES BIG QUESTIONS AT ALL-STAR PRESS CONFERENCE

"While the social media post was intended to be lighthearted, WNBA players are well aware of the league's policies prohibiting betting on WNBA games and receive training every year reinforcing those policies," the statement read.

"We recognized that the post missed the mark, removed it shortly after it was published, and addressed the matter internally. We will also use this as an opportunity to reemphasize with the players involved that conversations about wagering on WNBA games, even when intended as a joke, can have negative consequences."

It is unclear whether the statement's note that the matter was handled "internally" is in reference to the league having conversations with Reese and Bueckers about the clip or the individual who originally shared the video across the league's official social media. OutKick contacted the league for further clarification but did not immediately hear back.

When reached for comment about the video and any potential in-house investigations regarding the video, a Dream spokesperson told OutKick that the team has "no additional information to share other than what the league released." The Wings were not reached for comment.

Following Atlanta's 82-81 win on Wednesday, a laughing Reese joked that she would be requesting Bueckers' Apple Pay to receive her winnings from the wager.

Betting of any kind is strictly prohibited under the WNBA's new collective bargaining agreement, with Section 5 of Article 14 in the agreement dedicated to gambling regulations.

"Any player found by the Commissioner after a hearing to have been guilty of wagering (directly or indirectly), or of offering or attempting to wager, money or anything of value on the outcome, score, or any other aspect of any WNBA Competition shall, in the sole discretion of the Commissioner, be subject to a fine, suspension, and/or dismissal and disqualification from any further association with the WNBA," subsection c in the agreement reads.

While the WNBA described the wager between Bueckers and Reese as being "lighthearted," it was still a bet made between two players, caught on video, and shared across social media. One would think that WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert has the evidence to potentially impose punishments.

Other professional sports leagues have strict anti-gambling policies in place that carry severe punishments.

NFL players are prohibited from placing any wagers on NFL games. An NFL player wagering on an NFL game that does not involve his team carries an indefinite suspension of 1-year minimum, while wagering on your own team results in an indefinite two-year suspension.

In the MLB, if a player is found to be betting on games not involving their own team, the player is handed a one-year suspension. If found to be betting on games involving their own team, a lifetime ban is enforced under Major League Rule 21.

item.title: Older adults taking 5 or more prescription drugs face higher risk of death, study finds
item.description: Each additional prescription medication was linked to a 7% increase in death risk among older adults, raising urgent questions about deprescribing.
item.content:encoded:
Older adults who take five or more prescription medications face a significantly higher risk of death compared to those taking fewer drugs, according to a study published in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society.

The research highlights the growing concern over polypharmacy, the medical term for taking five or more daily prescriptions, and its long-term effects on aging populations.

Led by Dr. Alexander Chaitoff of the University of Michigan School of Medicine, researchers analyzed national survey data collected from 7,828 adults aged 65 and older between 1999 and 2016.

LONGER LIVES, WORSE HEALTH? SCIENTISTS UNCOVER TROUBLING TREND ACROSS GENERATIONS

Trained staff directly inspected participants' pill bottles to verify medication use over the previous 30 days, then followed them for an average of 8.5 years, according to a press release.

More than half of participants (54.3%) fell into at least one high-risk medication category. The largest group consisted of older adults taking five or more prescription drugs (polypharmacy).

Another group, 37.6% of those studied, used medications deemed risky for older individuals, such as drugs that can increase the risk of confusion or falls, the study revealed.

DOCTORS REVEAL HIDDEN DANGER FOR SOME OZEMPIC, WEGOVY USERS WITH BRAIN DISORDERS

Additionally, 11.4% took combinations of medications that are known to cause major drug-to-drug interactions.

After accounting for overall health and underlying conditions, taking five or more prescriptions was associated with a 38% increase in overall mortality risk. Each additional prescription medication added to a patient’s routine was linked to a 7% increase in death risk.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Taking multiple medications has been shown to increase the likelihood of side effects, adverse drug reactions and accidental overdose, particularly as the liver and kidneys age and process drugs less efficiently, according to medical experts at Cleveland Clinic.

The total number of medications participants took was the strongest independent predictor of mortality, even after accounting for drug-to-drug interactions and potentially inappropriate prescriptions.

These findings could help doctors determine which patients are the best candidates for "deprescribing," or carefully reducing or stopping unnecessary medications, the researchers stated.

The authors noted several limitations, including that the study focused strictly on community-dwelling older adults, excluding those living in nursing homes or assisted care facilities.

Additionally, medication use was documented during a single 30-day snapshot at the start of the study, meaning researchers could not track subsequent changes in prescriptions or evolving health conditions over time.

Experts emphasized that observational studies show association rather than direct causation. Older adults taking higher numbers of prescriptions often suffer from multiple severe or complex health conditions, which independently carry a higher mortality risk.

item.title: Savannah Bananas stars trade baseball dreams for kids' smiles: 'Exactly where God put me'
item.description: Savannah Bananas stars Reese Alexiades and DR Meadows open up about their unlikely baseball journeys, inspiring kids and why Alexiades says it's "exactly where God put me."
item.content:encoded:
Reese Alexiades and DR Meadows had baseball dreams just like the rest of us – getting to the major leagues. But their journeys took them on a route unimaginable even less than five years ago.

Alexiades played college ball at Pepperdine University, while Meadows played for Division II school Columbus State. Neither played minor league ball, but they now play in front of one of the largest baseball crowds ever.

Alexiades and Meadows hit the big time in another way, becoming stars for the Savannah Bananas. Meadows is the organization's all-time leader in "trick plays," while Alexiades plays with a cape on.

Despite selling out MLB ballparks and even playing in front of six-figure crowds at football stadiums, baseball purists will never get on board – unless, Alexiades says, "if they came to a game and caught an out." (If a fan catches a ball on the fly, the batter is out.)

But what fans do not understand the most, Meadows says, is that, contrary to popular belief, their games are not "scripted" like, say, the Harlem Globetrotters.

"There's a huge difference. In our league, all our teams are out to win. We're very competitive... Just this past weekend, we lost two out of three in Chicago against the Firefighters, and our guys were not happy," Meadows told Fox News Digital in a recent interview. "At the end of the day, we're there for a bigger picture: to put on a show for the fans, break down the wall for the kids there and put smiles on faces. That's what makes Banana Ball beautiful. Even though we get to have fun competing, winning and losing, we still get to make somebody's day."

No one Meadows and Alexiades' age grew up wanting to be Bananas – but that may have changed by now.

"One of the big reasons why I fell in love with baseball is looking up to other players. Now kids can look up to us, and what we're all about is bringing fun to the game of baseball. Kids being able to see us and see how much fun we have, that's what it's all about. We try to be the best role models we can be for kids because the kids are what it's all about," Alexiades said.

Meadows added, "You see kids at the Little League World Series listing their favorite players, and some are Bananas players. To know we have that kind of platform — and like Reese was saying, it all comes from having fun, playing the game and having fun. Youth sports these days should be less pressure and a lot more fun. I think it's cool that kids are getting to see how much fun we have and get to take that to their own game."

FORMER SAVANNAH BANANAS PLAYER NAMED MLB ALL-STAR, HOURS AFTER HITTING FOR CYCLE AS A ROOKIE

Alexiades and Meadows recently visited a children's hospital in Tennessee to give them some Dairy Queen, and on Thursday, for every Blizzard bought at select locations, at least $1 will be donated to Children’s Miracle Network to help support local children’s hospitals.

"That's the beauty of our platform and this partnership: We can really make an impact, and so can other people," Alexiades said.

"Getting to see those kids, put a smile on their faces, bring them Blizzard Treats and enjoy those with them was super cool. The amount of joy DQ brings and the Bananas bring – it all made sense," added Meadows.

So, while it may not be the big time they originally envisioned, it's the 2026 version of the big time, which is just fine with the baseball player in a cape – literally and figuratively.

"The whole goal is to be able to play the game we love for as long as we can. A lot of us, me included, and people in this organization have been told no at some point in their careers. The Bananas have given me a chance to keep going, keep playing and realize that it's for a bigger purpose now," Alexiades said.

"I get to go and probably have more fun than I would have ever had if I played in the major leagues. So I'm having the time of my life, and this is exactly where God put me."

Other footage shows crowds of migrants emerging from the sea, climbing up onto Ceuta's rocky shores and working their way around border fences.

Ceuta’s government, in its request for a national emergency declaration, noted that immigration from Morocco is always a problem for the Spanish enclave but claimed the last 10 days represented a peak "of particular intensity." That peak has seen more than 2,000 migrants cross the border in the past 10 days, Ceuta officials said, according to El País.

"The Government of Spain is fully committed to providing an immediate response to the situation in Ceuta. Sánchez, for his part, has claimed that accepting migrants is necessary to keep Spain's economy alive, arguing the country's low birth rates necessitate accepting immigrants.

"The West needs people. Currently, few of its countries have a rising population growth rate," Sánchez wrote in a February op-ed in The New York Times.

"Unless they embrace migration, they will experience a sharp demographic decline that will prevent them from keeping their economies and public services afloat. Their gross domestic product will stagnate. Their public healthcare and pension systems will suffer. 

"Neither AI nor robots will be able to prevent this outcome. ... The only option to avoid decline is to integrate migrants in the most orderly and effective way possible."
